buddhau sidhyati | nanu pariṇāmadharmatālakṣaṇā kriyā mā bhūdātmano vāstavī, bhoktṛtāpitu kiṃ na pāramārthikī | omityāha natu ātmanaḥ iti | cinmātrataiva, na viṣayopabhoktṛtā | naca tadatiriktamasya rūpamucitamiti hi uktaṃ vistarataḥ | nanu ahaṃkāreṇa evamātmā bhoktṛtvena abhoktaiva san vyavahriyatām | vyavahriyamāṇasya tu kathamasau bhogo bhavet | upacāre hi na upacāryasya svātmani viśeṣaḥ kaścit, apitu upacaritureva tathābhūta- buddhiśabdaviśeṣapratilambhātmā vyavahāraḥ, anyathā anantapramātṛbhedena yugapadupacaryamāṇāgnijalādiviruddhabhāvabheditavapurmāṇavako'pi anantaviruddharūpatāmekatrāpi kṣaṇe pratipadyet | tadetat pariharati ahaṃkāravyavahāryātmanā iti | kena etaduktaṃ-cidrūpatādhikaḥ kaścit puruṣasya bhoga iti | buddhibodhaṃ hi yadātmani aviśiṣṭatayā ahaṃkāro vyavaharati, sa eva ayaṃ bhogaḥ | citpratibimbayogini viṣayapratibimbavati ca buddhitattve ahamidaṃ jānāmi iti cetanācetanapratibimbadvayamelanāvyavahā- rakāriṇā ahaṃkāratattvena yo'bhimāno janitaḥ, sa eva buddhitattvāt tadvṛttyadhyavasāyagocarīkṛtastadbuddhipratibimbacittattvena saha ekāśrayatālakṣaṇaṃ saṃyogaṃ bhajamānaścittattvasya citpratibimbādanadhya- vasitabhedatvena bhoga iti ucyate | kāṇādādidarśane'pi hi jñānātmako guṇa ātmano'nyaḥ | kathaṃ tasya bhogaḥ | samavāyāditi cet, saṃbandhamātraṃ tarhi bhogarūpatāyāṃ kāraṇamiti uktaṃ bhavati | ihāpi ca darśitaḥ saṃbandhaścittatvādanadhyavasitabhedasya citpratibimbasya viṣayapratibimbena saha ahaṃkāramelitasya tayaiva buddhyā adhyavasitasya ekabuddhyāśrayatvalakṣaṇasaṃyoga iti saṃsargamātraprabhāvito'yaṃ bhogavyavahāraḥ sarvatra | (page 156) saṃsargaśca prāptilakṣaṇaḥ saṃyogo'stu samavāyo vā abhimānena vādāntareṇa | yadi vā tathābhūtasya saṃyogasya pūrvapūrvapralayamahā- pralayeṣu api prāthamyaṃ na avadhāryate iti anādiḥ saṃyogo bhavan samavāyāt na viśiṣyate | buddhitattvasya ca sarvo'yaṃ dharmaḥ | dharmadharmiṇośca yaḥ saṃbandhaḥ, sa saṃyoga iti vā tādātmyamiti vā samavāya iti vā ucyatām | vastuni labdhe hi saṃjñāsu kriyāsu
**Enjoyment is the meeting of two reflections** What is it to enjoy — to experience an object? The schools have their answers: the Sāṃkhya makes the cognition a transformation of matter; the Vaiśeṣika makes it a quality of the self joined to the object by a mysterious relation called inherence (samavāya). Abhinavagupta cuts through all of this with a single image: enjoyment is the *union of two reflections* — the reflection of consciousness and the reflection of the object — meeting in the intellect, and fused by the ego into the one act "I know this." Consider what happens when you know the blue. The intellect (buddhi) bears two reflections: the reflection of consciousness — the light itself, as it is present in the act of knowing — and the reflection of the blue, the object. The ego (ahaṅkāra) mixes them into the single conceit "I know this," and that conceit — the two reflections joined, determined by the intellect, resting in the one consciousness — is the enjoyment. The self, in itself, is not really an enjoyer; it is consciousness-mere. It is the ego that makes it appear as one who enjoys. And this is not a mere figure of speech in the loose sense: if it were, then by the infinite division of knowers, the same body could be dealt with at once as fire and water, as contradictory things, in a single moment — which is absurd. The enjoyment is real, but real as this union of reflections in the one consciousness. Now the Vaiśeṣika says: the cognition is a quality of the self, and it is joined to the object by inherence (samavāya). But Abhinavagupta's point is that the mere *relation* does all the work. If the cognition-quality is other than the self, then how is it enjoyed? "By inherence," the Vaiśeṣika says. But then the relation alone is the cause of the enjoyment-form — and that is precisely our point. Here too there is a relation: the consciousness-reflection, the object-reflection, the ego's mixing, the intellect's determining — the union in the one support. And the union is enough. Whether you call it conjunction (saṃyoga) or inherence (samavāya) matters not at all; once the thing is understood, the word is a mere label. And if the conjunction's beginning is not to be found in the prior dissolutions, then the conjunction, being beginningless, is not distinct from the inherence. Either way, in every view, the enjoyment-dealing is *relation-made* — saṃsargakṛta. So the deep point is this. Enjoyment is not a transaction between a self and a thing across a gap; it is the meeting, within the one light, of the light and the object's reflection, fused by the ego into "I know this." The relation — whatever we name it — is the whole of it. And this is why the consciousness-reflection and the object-reflection, wherever they meet in the intellect, stand in the support-supported relation, even to the point where one might call it inherence — without any contradiction. The enjoyment of the world is, in the end, the self-luminous light meeting its own reflections in the one act of knowing. ---

> The upoddhāta k6 & k8 state the core claim: consciousness (caitanya) is ajaḍā — non-inert, not a > passive thing. The seed of the crystal-argument (IPK 1.5.11): a consciousness that merely reflected > objects without knowing that it reflected them would be no different from a crystal — it would show, > but be inert. What distinguishes consciousness from the inert is that it is aware of itself in the > very act of manifesting. The claim grounds the whole refusal to treat consciousness as a product of > inert matter, and it is the same argument the Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi develops at length.
